theme: The offerings of the leaders, devotion in detail
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 7:1-89. This is the longest chapter in the book, and it records the same offering twelve times. Read it with patience, and ask why the Holy Spirit would give so much space to repetition.
settingTheScene: The tabernacle has been set up and anointed. Now the twelve tribal leaders bring gifts for its dedication: carts and oxen for the Levites, and then, one leader per day for twelve days, an identical offering of silver and gold vessels, animals, and grain. It is the last event in the book before the departure from Sinai, and it is the longest chapter of Numbers. It ends with a short note about Moses hearing the voice of God from the mercy seat.
observation: The leaders bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen as an offering (7:1-3).
God tells Moses to give the wagons to the Levites, according to their needs (7:4-9).
Each leader brings an offering on his own day: “Nahshon the son of Amminadab of the tribe of Judah” first (7:12).
Each offering is the same: a silver plate, a silver basin, a golden dish of incense, animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings (7:13-17).
The text repeats the list for each of the twelve tribes (7:18-83).
The total is added up at the end (7:84-88).
The Kohathites receive no wagons, because their duty is to carry the holy things on their shoulders (7:9).
“And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony” (7:89).
interpretation:
The repetition in this chapter is the point. Each tribe brings exactly the same gift, even though some were large and some small, and some were wealthy and some poor. No one tries to outdo the others. No one is left out. The identical gifts say that every tribe has an equal share in the worship of God. Judah, the leading tribe, and Naphtali, one of the smallest, are written down with the same lines.

The chapter also shows that God notices every gift. Twelve times the same words are written out in full. A modern editor would have said “the other tribes did likewise.” But God gives each leader his own paragraph, because each gift is individually received and individually remembered. Nothing given to God is lost in a crowd.

The detail about the wagons is easy to miss. The leaders give the Levites what they need to do their work. The Levites in the families of Gershon and Merari get wagons and oxen, in proportion to their burden. The Kohathites, whose task is the holiest, get none, because the holy things must be carried on the shoulder. The offerings of the people serve the needs of the ministry, and every task has its own tools.

The chapter ends quietly with a verse that is easy to pass over: Moses enters the tent of meeting and hears the voice of God. This is the answer to the whole purpose of the tabernacle. All the gifts, the carts, the silver, and the animals lead to a place where God speaks to his servant. The worship and generosity of the people make room for God’s voice.

It may feel strange to read the same list twelve times. But treat it as a reminder that no act of devotion is trivial to God.
connection: Jesus praised the widow who gave two small coins, because she gave more than the rich (Mark 12:41-44). Paul wrote that “each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give” (2 Corinthians 9:7), and that the church is a body in which every member matters (1 Corinthians 12). Hebrews 4:16 says that we can approach “the throne of grace” with confidence. Jesus speaks to us from heaven by his word.
application:
Reflect on whether you compare your giving to others. Ask God to make you content to give what he has put in your hand.

Remember that God notices what you do in secret. Offer something to him today that no one else will see.

Ask the Lord to speak to you through his Word, as he did to Moses.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you give without comparing yourself to others.
Thank him that he remembers each gift.
Thank him that he speaks to you through his Word.
